title: A derivation aloud
objectives: Derive the Black-Scholes equation aloud inside five minutes, justifying each step.

screens.prose: A candidate answers the question below. The interviewer marks the reasoning as much as the result. Three lines lose marks: silence, a dropped term, and a step with no reason.

params.title: Interview
lines: Interviewer: Derive the Black-Scholes equation. Five minutes, talk as you go.
You: Sure. The share follows dS = mu S dt + sigma S dW.
(You write for forty seconds and say nothing.)
You: By Ito, dV = (V_t + mu S V_S) dt + sigma S V_S dW.
You: I sell one option and hold Delta shares. The dW coefficient is sigma S (Delta - V_S), so I choose Delta = V_S and the noise cancels.
You: Now the book earns r dt, so V_t + r S V_S - r V = 0.
You: As a check, a forward satisfies it, because V_SS = 0.

screens.question: Tap the three lines that lose marks.

hints.text: One line has no words at all.
Compare line 4 with Itô's lemma: a term is missing.
Line 6 states a result with no "because".

feedback.correct: Silence (line 3), the missing $\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS}$ (line 4) and "earns $r$" with no reason (line 6).
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a gap in speech, a missing term, and a claim with no "because".

byKey.l1: You tapped the interviewer. Only the candidate's lines are marked.
byKey.l2: You tapped the model line. It is correct and states what is assumed.
byKey.l5: You tapped the hedge. It gives a reason: the $dW$ coefficient vanishes at $\Delta = V_S$.
byKey.l7: You tapped the check. A forward is the right quick test.

explain.text: Silence gives the interviewer nothing to mark. Line 4 drops $\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS}$ because $(dW)^2 = dt$ was forgotten. Line 6 needs "no noise, so no arbitrage".

screens.prose: Now say it right. These are the lines a strong candidate says, in order, with the reason inside each. The five minutes split as 1, 2, 1 and 1. Leave out the two lines that lose marks.
screens.question: Put the spoken lines in order.

lines.text: One minute, model and lemma: $dS = \mu S\,dt + \sigma S\,dW$, so $dV = (V_t + \mu SV_S$ ${}+ \tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS})\,dt$ ${}+ \sigma SV_S\,dW$, because $(dS)^2 = \sigma^2S^2\,dt$.
Two minutes, hedge: sell one option, hold $\Delta$ shares. The $dW$ coefficient is $\sigma S(\Delta - V_S)$, so I choose $\Delta = V_S$, and the noise and $\mu$ cancel.
One minute, no arbitrage: the book has no noise, so it must earn $r$, or cash would beat it. So $d\Pi = r\Pi\,dt$.
Equate the $dt$ terms: $V_t + rSV_S$ ${}+ \tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS}$ ${}- rV = 0$, with $\mu$ gone.
One minute, check: a forward solves it, because $V_{SS} = 0$. I assumed constant $\sigma$, continuous hedging and no costs.
Write the final equation first, then fill in the steps behind it.
lines.why: A result with no route leaves the interviewer to supply the reasons. Say the route first, in order.

lines.text: Work silently, then read out the finished page.
lines.why: Silence gives nothing to mark, and a slip cannot be caught early. Every step needs its reason as you go.

hints.text: Follow the clock: 1, 2, 1, 1 minutes.
The equation comes after the no-arbitrage line, and the check comes last.

feedback.correct: That is the five-minute answer: lemma, hedge, no arbitrage, equation, check.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Model and lemma first, then hedge, then no arbitrage, then the equation, then the check.

byKey.x1: You led with the answer. A derivation goes from the model to the equation, one reason at a time.
byKey.x2: You worked in silence. The reasons are the marks, so say them as you write.
byKey.left-out: A line of the answer is in the Left out list. Only the two lines that lose marks belong there.

explain.text: Each line states a step and its reason in one breath. After the equation, the check shows the interviewer you can test your own result.

screens.prose: The interviewer interrupts at the hedge. Answer in one sentence.

params.title: Interview
lines: Interviewer: Why may you choose Delta = V_S?

screens.question: Which answer gets the marks?

options.text: $\Delta$ is mine to choose, and $V_S$ makes the $dW$ term zero
$V_S$ is the delta that dealers quote, so the market sets it, not me
options.why: You treated delta as a market quote. We build the book, and we choose $\Delta$ to kill the noise.

options.text: $V_S$ is the chance the option finishes in the money
options.why: You read delta as a probability. For our call it is $\Phi(d_1) = 0.6368$, not $\Phi(d_2) = 0.5596$.

options.text: any $\Delta$ works, because $dW$ has mean zero and averages out
options.why: You ignored leftover noise. With $\Delta \neq V_S$ the book is risky, so it need not earn $r$.

hints.text: Look at the $dW$ coefficient of the book: $\sigma S(\Delta - V_S)$.
Which $\Delta$ makes it zero?

feedback.correct: $\Delta$ is a free choice, and $V_S$ is the one that cancels the $dW$ term.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which choice makes the book riskless.

byKey.market: You made delta a market quote. It is a choice that removes the noise.
byKey.itm: You read delta as a chance. It is a hedge ratio, and it differs from $\Phi(d_2)$.
byKey.any: You said any $\Delta$ works. Only $\Delta = V_S$ leaves no noise.

explain.text: The $dW$ coefficient of the book is $\sigma S(\Delta - V_S)$. Setting it to zero is the whole reason for $\Delta = V_S$.

screens.prose: The interviewer asks why the hedged book earns $r$. A junior answers: "It holds shares, so it earns what shares earn, $\mu$." Give the reply that earns the marks.

params.title: Interview
lines: Interviewer: Why must the hedged book earn r?
Junior: It holds shares, so it earns mu.

screens.question: Which reply is right?

options.text: no noise is left, so any other return is a sure profit
shares earn $r$ on average, so the book earns $r$ too
options.why: You gave shares the return $r$. In the real world they earn $\mu$. The argument does not use their average return.

options.text: a hedge removes return as well as risk, so it earns zero
options.why: You assumed a hedge kills return. A riskless book still earns interest on its value.

options.text: $\Delta$ is fixed over the step, so the return is fixed at $r$
options.why: Holding $\Delta$ fixed is a modelling step. It does not set the return.

hints.text: What if the riskless book earned more than cash?
You could borrow cash and hold the book for a sure profit.

feedback.correct: Riskless means it earns $r$: a riskless book beating or trailing cash is an arbitrage.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what an investor could do if a riskless book earned more or less than cash.

byKey.mu: You gave the book the share's return. The share's $\mu$ cancelled with the noise.
byKey.zero: You said the hedge removes the return. It removes the risk only.
byKey.fixed: You pointed at the fixed $\Delta$. That is the set-up, not the reason.

explain.text: A book with no noise that earned more than $r$ would be a sure profit financed by cash. So it earns exactly $r$, and $\mu$ plays no part.

screens.prose: The interviewer notes that the answer has no $\mu$ in it, and asks where it went.

params.title: Interview
lines: Interviewer: So mu has disappeared. Where did it go?

screens.question: Which answer gets the marks?

options.text: $\mu$ is in $dV$ and in $\Delta\,dS$ with opposite signs, so it cancels
I assumed $\mu = r$ to keep the algebra short, as an approximation
options.why: You added an assumption. None is needed: $\mu$ cancels by itself.

options.text: $dW$ has mean zero, so $\mu$ averages out over the path
options.why: You averaged away $\mu$. It multiplies $dt$, not $dW$, so averaging leaves it. The hedge removes it.

options.text: discounting at $r$ absorbs $\mu$ into the present value
options.why: You blamed discounting. That uses $r$, and $\mu$ has gone before any discounting.

hints.text: Where does $\mu$ sit in $dV$?
And in $d\Pi = -dV + \Delta\,dS$? The signs are opposite.

feedback.correct: The share's drift appears in the option and in the shares, with opposite signs, and the hedge cancels it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at where $\mu$ appears in $dV$ and in $\Delta\,dS$.

byKey.assume: You assumed $\mu = r$. Nothing about $\mu$ is assumed.
byKey.mean: You averaged $\mu$ away. The cancellation is exact, path by path.
byKey.disc: You said discounting removes it. $\mu$ is gone before we discount.

explain.text: In $d\Pi = -dV + \Delta\,dS$ the $\mu$ terms are $-\mu SV_S$ and $+\mu S\Delta$. With $\Delta = V_S$ they cancel, so two investors who disagree about $\mu$ agree on the price.

screens.prose: Last interruption on the assumptions: "What if $\sigma$ is not constant?"

params.title: Interview
lines: Interviewer: What if sigma is not constant?

screens.question: Which answer gets the marks?

options.text: $\sigma(t, S)$ changes nothing; a random $\sigma$ needs a second hedge
Nothing changes whatever $\sigma$ does, because $\mu$ cancelled
options.why: You carried the cancellation of $\mu$ over to $\sigma$. A random $\sigma$ is a second source of noise that shares cannot hedge.

options.text: The equation fails for any $\sigma$ that is not constant
options.why: You said it fails for every non-constant $\sigma$. With $\sigma(t, S)$ the argument is intact.

options.text: $\sigma$ moves into the drift term, so $\mu$ returns to the price
options.why: You moved $\sigma$ into the drift. The new problem is noise from $\sigma$, not a drift.

hints.text: Does the hedge still cancel $dW$ if $\sigma = \sigma(t, S)$?
What if $\sigma$ had a noise of its own?

feedback.correct: With $\sigma(t, S)$ the same steps give the same equation. A stochastic $\sigma$ adds noise the share cannot hedge.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate a $\sigma$ that depends on $(t, S)$ from one with its own noise.

byKey.same: You said nothing changes. A random $\sigma$ needs its own hedge, such as another option.
byKey.fails: You said it fails always. A deterministic function $\sigma(t, S)$ keeps the argument.
byKey.drift: You moved $\sigma$ into the drift. The issue is unhedgeable noise.

explain.text: Local volatility $\sigma(t, S)$ keeps the same equation with $\sigma$ inside. Stochastic volatility needs a second hedging instrument, which is why vol desks use options to hedge vega.

screens.question: Fill in the four terms and their sum, to 4 decimal places.

hints.text: $\Theta$ has two pieces: the volatility piece and the interest piece.
Then add the four terms with the sign shown.

feedback.correct: $-6.4140 + 3.1842 + 3.7524$ ${}- 0.5225 = 0.0001$ from rounded terms, and $0$ before rounding.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute each term to 4 places, then add the first three and subtract $rV$.

byKey.r0c1: $\Theta = -3.7524 - 2.6616$ ${}= -6.4140$. The first piece is $S\varphi(d_1)\sigma/(2\sqrt{T})$ ${}= 3.7524$, the second $rKe^{-rT}\Phi(d_2) = 2.6616$.
byKey.r4c1: The four terms cancel: the sum is zero before rounding, and $0.0001$ from the rounded values.

explain.text: The terms are $\Theta = -6.4140$, $rS\Delta = 3.1842$, $\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma$ ${}= 3.7524$ and $rV = 0.5225$. Gamma earns what theta costs, less the interest the book owes.

screens.prose: Follow-up: "Check it on something simple." A forward $V = S - Ke^{-r(T - t)}$ has $V_{SS} = 0$, so the $\sigma$ term vanishes. Take $S = 80$, $K = 90$, $r = 3\%$ and half a year to go.
screens.question: What is $V_t$? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: $\dfrac{d}{dt}\big(-Ke^{-r(T - t)}\big)$ ${}= -rKe^{-r(T - t)}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Differentiate $-Ke^{-r(T - t)}$ with respect to $t$.

byKey.sign: You gave the right size with the wrong sign. As $t$ rises the strike's present value rises, so $V$ falls: $V_t < 0$.
byKey.no-discount: You gave $-rK = -2.7$, with no discount factor $e^{-r(T - t)} = 0.9851$.
byKey.zero: You set $V_t$ to zero because $V$ is linear in $S$. Time still moves the discounted strike.

explain.text: Then $V_t + rSV_S - rV = -2.6598$ ${}+ 2.4 + 0.2598 = 0$, with $V_{SS} = 0$ and $V = -8.6601$. In one sentence: a forward is linear in $S$, so only the bond term remains, and it balances.

screens.prose: Make the check executable. `pde_terms` returns $\Theta$, $rS\Delta$, $\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma$, $rV$ and the sum for a call. The sum is the equation's residual and must vanish.
screens.question: Complete `pde_terms`.

widget.how: Submit runs 6 hidden tests. They check the four terms to 4 places at three inputs, and the unrounded sum within 1e-10 of zero.

hints.text: $\Gamma$ ${}= \varphi(d_1)/(S\sigma\sqrt{T})$ and $\Delta = \Phi(d_1)$.
$\Theta$ ${}= -S\varphi(d_1)\sigma/(2\sqrt{T})$ ${}- rKe^{-rT}\Phi(d_2)$.
Return the list, then the sum of the first three minus the fourth.

feedback.correct: At the shared option the terms are $-6.4140$, $3.1842$, $3.7524$, $0.5225$, and the sum is zero to 1e-10.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the example: the terms are $-6.414$, $3.1842$, $3.7524$ and $0.5225$.

explain.text: A zero residual at three different markets is strong evidence that the equation and the formula agree. It is not a proof, and an interviewer knows it.

screens.prose: A strats final round. You finish the call and the interviewer says: "Now the put. Same hedge. What changes?" You have one minute.

params.title: Interview
lines: Interviewer: Now the put. Same hedge. What changes?

screens.question: Which answer gets the marks?

options.text: The equation is the same; only the condition at $T$ changes, to $\max(K - S, 0)$
The equation gains a minus sign on $rSV_S$ because $\Delta$ is negative
options.why: You moved the sign into the equation. A negative $\Delta$ is a value of $V_S$, and the equation holds it as is.

options.text: A put needs a fresh derivation with $\Delta = -V_S$
options.why: You started again. The argument never used the payoff, only that $V$ is a smooth function of $(t, S)$.

options.text: $\mu$ comes back because a put gains when the share falls
options.why: You brought $\mu$ back. The hedge cancels it for any claim, puts included.

hints.text: The derivation uses only that $V$ is smooth in $(t, S)$.
Where does the payoff enter?

feedback.correct: Same equation, different payoff at $T$: $V_t + rSV_S$ ${}+ \tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS}$ ${}- rV = 0$ with $V(T, S) = \max(K - S, 0)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which part of the derivation depends on the payoff?

byKey.sign: You changed the equation. It holds for any claim; the put's $V_S$ is simply negative.
byKey.new: You restarted. The derivation holds for any claim, so only the payoff at $T$ changes.
byKey.mu: You let $\mu$ back in. The hedge cancels it for any claim.

explain.text: Now answer it all aloud. The homework item "Derivation" asks for the five-minute derivation and two interviewer follow-ups, marked against a rubric.

ideas: Say the route first, with its reason in each line: model and lemma, hedge, no arbitrage, equation, check.
$\Delta = V_S$ cancels the $dW$ term and $\mu$ together; a noiseless book earns $r$, or cash would beat it.
The equation holds for any claim, puts and forwards included. Only the payoff at $T$ differs, and a forward has $V_{SS} = 0$.

formula.name: Black-Scholes equation
formula.note: Five minutes: lemma one, hedge two, arbitrage and equation one, check one.

summary.trap: Do not derive in silence or drop the Itô term. The reasons are the marks, and $\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS}$ is the whole gamma effect.

quiz.prose: A claim has $V = 8$ at $S = 80$, with $V_S = 0.5$ and $V_{SS} = 0.01$. Take $r = 4\%$ and $\sigma = 25\%$.
quiz.question: What must $V_t$ be for the equation to hold?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move $rSV_S$ and the gamma term to the other side of the equation.

byKey.no-gamma: You left out $\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2V_{SS}$ ${}= 2.0$. That is the Itô term again.
byKey.flipped: You kept the signs of the left side. Moving terms across changes their signs.

explain.text: The gamma term is $\tfrac12 \times 0.0625 \times 6400 \times 0.01$ ${}= 2.0$. With $rSV_S = 1.6$ and $rV = 0.32$, $V_t = -3.28$.

quiz.question: What is its $\Theta$ from the equation? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve the equation for $\Theta$ with the put's own $V$, $\Delta$ and $\Gamma$.

byKey.no-delta: You dropped $-rS\Delta$. For a put $\Delta$ is negative, so it adds $+2.7518$.
byKey.call: You gave the call's theta. The put has the same equation and its own numbers.
byKey.flipped: You flipped the sign. The put decays slightly: $\Theta < 0$.

explain.text: The same equation works for the put. Its negative $\Delta$ makes $-rS\Delta = +2.7518$.

quiz.prose: The interviewer asks: "Is $\Delta = V_S$ held fixed until expiry?"
quiz.question: Which answer gets the marks?

options.text: No: it is fixed only over $dt$, then reset to the new $V_S$
Yes: one hedge at the start lasts all the way to $T$
options.why: You said hedge once. As $S$ moves, $V_S$ moves, and the book picks up risk.

options.text: No: it is reset to the share's drift $\mu$ after each step
options.why: You swapped delta for $\mu$. The hedge ratio is always $V_S$.

options.text: Yes: gamma corrects the hedge automatically, with no trading
options.why: You said gamma fixes it. Gamma measures how fast $V_S$ changes. It does not rebalance anything.

feedback.correct: The hedge is rebalanced continuously: fixed over each $dt$, new at the next.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. $V_S$ changes as $S$ and $t$ change.

explain.text: Fixed over an instant is the modelling step. Rebalancing in practice is discrete, which is where hedging error comes from.

quiz.prose: A book has $\Gamma = 0.0125$ per call at $S = 100$, with $\sigma = 30\%$.
quiz.question: What is $\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2\Gamma$ per call, in £ a year?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $\tfrac12\sigma^2S^2 = 450$, then multiply by $\Gamma$.
